section_summary: This section documents repeated Japanese interception, censorship, opening, delay, and removal of American official and private mail in Japan, Japanese-occupied China, Taiwan, and French Indochina during 1940–1941. It includes cross-reference sheets, private and commercial complaints, State Department correspondence and instructions, consular reports, Japanese denials, and evidence that official covers, bank documents, letters, periodicals, checks, and parcel post were affected. The final documents describe Japan's October 1941 Temporary Postal Control Ordinance and the procedures under which diplomatic and consular correspondence could obtain limited exemptions.

subfiles.title: Refusal to Accept Mail Bearing U.S.A. Constitutional Commemoration Stamps
subfiles.from: Foochow (Ward)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a despatch concerning Japanese postal refusal of mail bearing U.S. commemorative stamps.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Foochow Despatch 149 to Peiping on refusal of U.S. Constitutional Commemoration stamps, file 893.713/53.

subfiles.title: Opening of American Official Mail Passing Through Japan
subfiles.from: American Embassy in Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a despatch reporting representations against the opening of American official mail.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: increasingly common opening of American official mail passing through Japan, with an Embassy representation May 31 to the Foreign Office's American Bureau director.

subfiles.title: Inquiry About a Censored Letter from Japan
subfiles.from: Mrs. J. D. Collier
subfiles.about: An American woman asks whether the United States or another country censored and left open a letter from her husband in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Collier says a letter from her husband in Yokohama bore signs of censorship and arrived improperly sealed, and asks whether American or other authorities opened it.

subfiles.title: Reply Concerning Censorship of a Letter from Japan
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department states that the United States had not instituted censorship of letters from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the U.S. wasn't censoring letters from Japan; since the censorship strip names no country, it may have been opened in Japan or Canada.

subfiles.title: Tampering with Official Covers from Tokyo
subfiles.from: Nagasaki (Tever)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to reports that official covers from the Consulate General at Tokyo showed evidence of tampering.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Nagasaki Despatch 200: several wax-sealed official covers from Tokyo showed unmistakable interference.

subfiles.title: Tampering with Official American Mail by Japanese Postal Authorities
subfiles.from: American Embassy in Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to correspondence with the Japanese Foreign Office about tampered American official mail.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: the Foreign Office found evidence of mail tampering insufficient while cases continued; a U.S. Treasury exemption for consular correspondence might encourage Japanese restraint.

subfiles.title: Tampering with Consular Mail at Tsingtao
subfiles.from: Tsingtao (Meyer)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a political report containing information about Japanese tampering with consular mail.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Tsingtao's October 1940 report on Japanese interference with consular mail.

subfiles.title: Japanese Translations of American Official Despatches
subfiles.from: American Embassy in Japan (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to information about Japanese translations of American official reports concerning Chiang Kai-shek and a prospective American loan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a telegram on a file of Japanese translations of American despatches about conversations with Chiang Kai-shek and others on a prospective loan.

subfiles.title: Registered Mail to Mukden and Harbin
subfiles.from: Dairen (Cheee)
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to difficulties transmitting registered mail to Mukden and Harbin.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a telegram on obstacles to registered mail to the Mukden and Harbin consulates and using Manchurian offices to exchange confidential messages with Dairen.

subfiles.title: Detention in Japan of Chase Bank Registered Mail
subfiles.from: Siegfried Stern, Chase National Bank
subfiles.to: Dean G. Acheson, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Chase National Bank requests diplomatic help recovering valuable registered mail detained in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stern says registered mail from Chase Bank's Tientsin and Shanghai offices, sent on Japanese ships between June 15 and July 30, was believed detained in Japan, holding drafts and shipping documents worth over a million dollars needed to collect on letters of credit.

subfiles.title: Department Reply to Chase Bank on Detained Registered Mail
subfiles.from: Walter A. Adams, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The Department requests registration numbers before instructing the Ambassador in Tokyo to intervene.
subfiles.summary: Adams acknowledges the bank's report that mail from Tientsin and Shanghai was being detained in Japan. He asks for registration numbers to facilitate identification but promises that, even if they are unavailable, the Ambassador will be asked to make representations using the information already supplied.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Protest Japanese Interference with American Mail
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, via Peiping; repeated to Peiping, Chungking, Shanghai, and Canton
subfiles.about: The Department orders an emphatic protest against Japanese interference with American mail and seeks release of Chase Bank documents.
subfiles.summary: Telegram cites flagrant continuing interference with American mail, including Chase documents held in Japan; the Embassy must demand an end in Japan and occupied China and stress Japanese mail in the U.S. wasn't treated similarly.

subfiles.title: Legal Basis for Statement on U.S. Postal Censorship
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum explains why a draft protest states that Japanese mail was not similarly censored in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Memo: U.S. law didn't authorize postal censorship, though obscene material could be held unopened; the draft rejects any Japanese attempt to refer interference in occupied China to Nanking authorities.

subfiles.title: Chase Bank Follow-up on Missing Registration Numbers
subfiles.from: Siegfried Stern, Chase Bank
subfiles.to: Walter A. Adams, Department of State
subfiles.about: The bank reports that it cannot yet supply registration numbers and asks that diplomatic representations proceed.
subfiles.summary: Stern says repeated cables to Chase's Far Eastern branches haven't produced registration numbers, which may never come, so he asks the Department to have the Ambassador intervene on the original information.

subfiles.title: Japanese Censorship of a Mission Letter to the Canton Consulate General
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Myers reports the apparent removal of official communications from a registered letter mailed by the American Presbyterian Mission at Hoihow.
subfiles.summary: A registered airmail letter from Hoihow arrived containing only an unsealed inner envelope and blank paper, while four telegram confirmations and other correspondence were missing. Japanese military authorities denied censoring the letter, but Myers found the denial unsatisfactory and concluded that further local representations would probably be fruitless.

subfiles.title: Protest over the Hoihow Mission Letter
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Canton
subfiles.about: The Consulate protests the apparent removal of documents from an official letter sent from Hoihow.
subfiles.summary: Protest over the Hoihow mission letter: the registered cover arrived blank, lacking the telegram confirmations and letters, suggesting censorship at Hoihow or Canton; it asks safeguards against further interference with official American mail.

subfiles.title: Japanese Denial of Censoring the Hoihow Letter
subfiles.from: T. Takatsu, Japanese Consul General, Canton
subfiles.to: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Takatsu relays the Japanese military authorities' denial that they censored the registered letter from Hoihow.
subfiles.summary: Takatsu acknowledges the American memorandum and later letter on the registered airmail cover and says a military investigation found no censorship.

subfiles.title: Rejection of the Japanese Reply on the Hoihow Letter
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.to: T. Takatsu, Japanese Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Myers rejects the Japanese military authorities' answer as unsatisfactory.
subfiles.summary: Myers corrects Takatsu: the cover was addressed to the Canton office, not Hong Kong, and given the evidence the Consulate General can't accept the military denial.

subfiles.title: Department Note on Censorship of Consular Mail at Dairen
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: An internal note summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5811 and the Foreign Office's dismissive response to mail opening at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The note records that Despatch No. 5811 enclosed a conversation about the opening of consular mail by a censor. It highlights a Foreign Office official's joke that Japanese should be sent to the United States to learn how to open mail expertly.

subfiles.title: Censorship of American Consular Mail at Dairen
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports that the Embassy protested the opening of consular mail at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy took up the Dairen Consul's August 8 report immediately with the Japanese Foreign Office. Grew encloses the responsible Embassy officer's memorandum and promises to transmit any substantive Japanese reply.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Shiroji Yuki on Dairen Mail Censorship
subfiles.from: H. Merrell Benninghoff
subfiles.about: Benninghoff records his discussion with Shiroji Yuki about an official envelope opened at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Benninghoff gave Shiroji Yuki the opened Dairen envelope and asked him to stop censorship and police activities; Yuki admitted it was opened, expressed little optimism, and joked Japanese were learning to open mail more skillfully.

subfiles.title: Institution of Comprehensive Foreign-Mail Censorship in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports an imperial ordinance authorizing comprehensive censorship of foreign mail.
subfiles.summary: The official gazette authorized the Communications Minister to institute comprehensive postal censorship; papers said opening and inspection of all foreign mail would begin October 20 against alleged espionage and propaganda.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy Reply to Protests over Mail Interference in North China
subfiles.from: Richard P. Butrick, American Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.about: Butrick transmits the Japanese Embassy's denial of censorship and discriminatory delay of American mail in North China.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese reply denied opening official mail for the consulates at Chefoo and Tsingtao or blocking American periodicals and mail in Fenchow. It attributed any delays to military necessity and rejected allegations of discriminatory treatment, after which the American Embassy concluded that further representations in Peiping would be unproductive.

subfiles.title: Removal and Attempted Use of Gertrude Hill's Check
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Myers reports that a check stolen from Gertrude Hill's mail was fraudulently tendered at a Canton shoe shop.
subfiles.summary: A man used a HK$20 check payable to Gertrude Hill, reclaimed it, and it later reached Hill anonymously with a note saying it was found; Myers believes Japanese censors removed it and suspects the Gendarmerie, while Japanese consular police couldn't identify the offender.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Check Removed from Gertrude Hill's Mail
subfiles.from: American Consulate General, Canton
subfiles.about: The Consulate requests an investigation of the theft and attempted use of a check mailed to Gertrude Hill.
subfiles.summary: Memo reconstructs the check's presentation at Y. A. Wahab's shop, its recovery by an unidentified customer and anonymous delivery to Hill, concludes her mail was tampered with, and asks the culprit be caught and recurrence prevented.

subfiles.title: Japanese Consul General's Reply on Gertrude Hill's Mail
subfiles.from: T. Takatsu, Japanese Consul General, Canton
subfiles.to: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Takatsu reports that Japanese consular police had not found the person responsible for tampering with Hill's mail.
subfiles.summary: Takatsu says police investigated the case in the June 17 memorandum, the person wasn't located, and Hill's letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Final Japanese Reply on Violations of Consular Mail
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a final reply from the Japanese Consulate General concerning violations of a consulate's mail.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a final Japanese reply on violations of consular mail was enclosed with another document; despatch number, post and date illegible.

subfiles.title: Referral of Hanoi Despatch on Parcel Post Detention
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The Far Eastern Division refers Hanoi's report on detained parcel post for possible transmission to postal authorities.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Hanoi air-mail Despatch 254 (November 3, 1941): suggests the communications division send a copy to postal authorities.

subfiles.title: Detention of Parcel Post Shipments at Haiphong
subfiles.from: Charles S. Reed II, American Consulate, Hanoi
subfiles.about: The Hanoi Consulate reports Japanese detention of approximately 7,000 sacks of parcel post intended for unoccupied China.
subfiles.summary: The sacks were part of a larger shipment previously passed by Japanese authorities, but officials refused either to forward them or consistently implement proposals for their return or auction. A Chinese Postal Service representative believed the authorities were waiting for the Yoshizawa Mission before deciding the shipment's fate.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Hanoi Parcel-Post Report to the Postmaster General
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Postmaster General a copy of the Hanoi despatch on parcel post detained at Haiphong.
subfiles.summary: Formal note sends the Postmaster General Despatch 254 from the Hanoi consul on Japanese detention of parcel-post shipments in Indochina.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Tsinan Despatch on Interference with Official Mail
subfiles.from: Richard P. Butrick, American Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.about: The Peiping Embassy forwards a Tsinan report on continuing interference with American official mail.
subfiles.summary: Butrick encloses Tsinan Despatch No. 382 but notes that no additional representation was made to the Japanese Embassy on its basis. Despite earlier unresponsive Japanese replies, the Embassy had recently observed a slight improvement in mail conditions.

subfiles.title: Tampering with Official American Mail Continues
subfiles.from: Carl J. Hawthorne, American Vice Consul, Tsinan
subfiles.to: Clarence K. Gauss, American Ambassador, Peiping
subfiles.about: The Tsinan Consulate reports worsening opening and delay of American official and private mail.
subfiles.summary: Wax-sealed official covers from Tientsin, Peiping, Shanghai and Tsingtao showed opening, so Hawthorne recommends couriers, lock-sealed envelopes or double covers for confidential material; Tsinan-Tsingtao mail was delayed or lost, and Americans' mail was routinely opened and held.

subfiles.title: Exemption of Consular Communications from the Temporary Postal Control Ordinance
subfiles.from: Glen Bruner, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Bruner transmits Taiwan regulations governing exemptions for consular mail under Japan's new postal-control system.
subfiles.summary: The Taihoku Consulate registered its seal with the Central Post Office and apparently won most exemptions from the Temporary Postal Control Ordinance; stamp-affixing before a clerk stayed disputed, and incoming foreign mail and packages still suffered delay or detention.

subfiles.title: Conditions for Consular-Mail Exemptions in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Teruo Hachiya, Government General of Taiwan
subfiles.to: Glen Bruner, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: The Taiwan Government General specifies markings and registration procedures for exempt consular mail.
subfiles.summary: Consular-mail exemptions in Taiwan require a responsible person, official seal or signature, registered sample covers and a designated post office; named officers may use similar procedures, but propaganda on national policy or war conditions isn't covered.

subfiles.title: Confirmation of Exempt Provisions for Consular Mail
subfiles.from: Morizo Morita, Government General of Taiwan
subfiles.about: The Government General identifies the postal-control provisions inapplicable to properly registered consular and diplomatic mail.
subfiles.summary: Morita says once the October 23 formalities are completed, Government General Ordinances 199 and 200 and Article II of the imperial ordinance won't apply to designated consular mail.

subfiles.title: Government General Ordinance No. 199
subfiles.from: Kiyoshi Hasegawa, Governor-General of Taiwan
subfiles.to: Public and postal authorities in Taiwan
subfiles.about: The ordinance prohibits several methods of secret communication in foreign mail while allowing designated exemptions.
subfiles.summary: Government General Ordinance 199, effective October 20, 1941, bars codes, secret ink, private postcards and double envelopes in mail abroad, with exemptions at the Governor-General's discretion.

subfiles.title: Government General Ordinance No. 200
subfiles.from: Kiyoshi Hasegawa, Governor-General of Taiwan
subfiles.to: Public and postal authorities in Taiwan
subfiles.about: The ordinance prescribes identification, postage, translation, and verification requirements for foreign mail.
subfiles.summary: Senders had to display names and addresses clearly and present unattached postage stamps with foreign mail. Postal authorities could demand translations or proof of identity, although the Governor-General could exempt designated persons or mail; the rules took effect October 20, 1941.

subfiles.title: Extract from the Temporary Postal Control Ordinance
subfiles.from: Imperial Government of Japan
subfiles.about: Article II authorizes wartime censorship of mail while exempting certain government and domestic correspondence.
subfiles.summary: Extract from the Temporary Postal Control Ordinance: the Communications Minister may order wartime mail censorship to protect defense; exempt are marked government mail and certain sealed domestic documents, except suspicious or extraterritorial correspondence.
